# Pat Moriarty - Volunteer & Community Coordinator

## My Role at Horizon Foundation

I'm the person who keeps our volunteer army of 85 people organised, motivated, and coming back for more. It's honestly like herding cats sometimes, but I absolutely love it. My day usually starts at 7:30am checking emails from volunteers — someone's sick and can't do their shift at the Rockingham op shop, another needs their Working With Children check renewed, or a new person wants to know more about helping out.

I spend about 60% of my time on volunteer coordination — recruiting, interviewing, onboarding, rostering, and what I call "volunteer wellbeing." That means making sure our amazing volunteers feel valued, not taken for granted. The other 40% is split between running our community events (which are goldmines for finding new volunteers and donors) and coordinating our social enterprise operations. That's our three op shops in Rockingham, Armadale, and Midland, plus the Good Work Café in Fremantle that trains young people in hospitality skills.

People don't realise how complex volunteer management actually is. I'm not just making rosters — though God knows that's complicated enough with 85 people across 12 programs. I'm doing performance management when volunteers aren't pulling their weight, mediating conflicts between strong personalities, and constantly training people on everything from child protection to how our client database works. Last month alone I conducted 14 volunteer interviews and onboarded 7 new people.

The social enterprise side keeps growing, which is exciting but also terrifying. The op shops generated $68,000 last year, and the café brought in another $45,000 while training 23 young people. But every time Maya talks about expanding these operations, I think about who's actually going to run them day-to-day. It's not just about finding more volunteers — it's about finding the *right* volunteers who can handle retail customers or work alongside vulnerable young people.

## Facts I Know

Our volunteer program is honestly one of the most robust in the sector, though I say that with a mix of pride and exhaustion. We have 85 active volunteers contributing about 8,400 hours annually — that's roughly $420,000 worth of labour if we had to pay for it at minimum wage. The Red Cross taught me to track everything, so I know these numbers cold.

Our volunteer retention rate is 78% year-on-year, which is pretty good compared to the sector average of around 65%. But that means we're still losing nearly a quarter of our volunteers annually, so recruitment never stops. I run volunteer information sessions every six weeks, and we get about 12-15 people each time. Maybe half of those actually follow through with an application.

The Working With Children checks are a constant juggling act — 67 of our volunteers need them for their roles, and they expire every three years. I have a colour-coded spreadsheet that tracks renewal dates because letting someone's check lapse means they can't work with our youth employment program or the digital literacy sessions. The Department of Communities takes about 6-8 weeks to process renewals, so I start chasing people three months early.

Our op shops are performing really well considering they're volunteer-run. Rockingham is our star performer — it brought in $28,400 last year because it's in a great location and has this core team of six volunteers who've been there since we opened. Midland does about $22,100 annually, and Armadale struggles a bit at $17,500 because the foot traffic isn't as good. 

The Good Work Café is my baby project that sometimes keeps me awake at night. We train 20-25 young people annually through our partnership with South Metropolitan TAFE, and 89% of them complete the program. But the café only breaks even financially — last year we had $45,200 in revenue against $44,800 in costs. Jess keeps saying the value is in the training outcomes, not the profit, but Craig gets twitchy about anything that doesn't contribute to the bottom line.

## My Opinions

Here's what I've learned in four years: volunteers are the absolute heart of this organisation, and if we don't treat them that way, we're screwed. I came from Red Cross where volunteer management was taken seriously — proper systems, recognition programs, clear role descriptions. When I started at Horizon, volunteers were basically an afterthought. People would just assume volunteers would show up and do whatever needed doing.

I've worked hard to professionalise how we work with volunteers, but I'm still fighting against this attitude that volunteer coordination is somehow less important than program delivery. When Jess needs someone to run a digital literacy session in Bunbury and I tell her our volunteers aren't available, she acts like I'm being difficult instead of managing a complex workforce.

The training café desperately needs a proper paid manager, not just volunteer coordination. Right now it's run by a mix of TAFE trainers, volunteers, and whoever from our team has time. That's not sustainable if we want to expand. These young people deserve consistency and professional support, not whoever happens to be rostered on. I keep pushing Maya on this, but the response is always "where's the funding going to come from?"

Our volunteer recognition is getting better, but it's still not where it should be. The annual volunteer appreciation dinner is nice, but people need to feel valued year-round. I started a "Volunteer Spotlight" in our newsletter and created little milestone gifts — coffee vouchers for 50 hours, Horizon branded keep cups for 100 hours. Sounds small, but the feedback has been incredible.

One thing that really frustrates me: we lose good volunteers because they feel taken for granted or their concerns aren't heard. Last year we lost Margaret, who'd been running our Armadale op shop for three years, because she asked for a proper security system after a break-in and nothing happened for months. When volunteers are giving their time for free, the least we can do is listen to their reasonable requests.

## Working at Horizon Foundation

Maya Thompson is a brilliant CEO who genuinely cares about volunteers, but she's pulled in so many directions that volunteer issues don't always get the attention they deserve. She totally gets the big picture — she'll talk about volunteers as "essential infrastructure" in board meetings — but when it comes to approving spending on volunteer management systems or recognition programs, there's always something more urgent.

Jess Warburton and I have an interesting relationship. She's incredibly passionate about program delivery and outcomes, which I respect enormously. But she sometimes sees volunteers as just extra hands rather than people with their own motivations and needs. We've had some frank conversations about this. She's gotten better at giving volunteers meaningful roles instead of just asking them to stuff envelopes.

Craig Donovan drives me a bit crazy with his spreadsheet obsession, but I actually appreciate his attention to detail. He helped me build better systems for tracking volunteer hours and calculating the dollar value of volunteer contributions. That data has been crucial for grant applications. But he definitely doesn't understand why I spend money on volunteer appreciation events or training materials.

Amara Osei is brilliant to work with because she totally gets that happy volunteers are great ambassadors for the organisation. Some of our best individual donors came through volunteers talking about their experience. She's helped me frame volunteer management as part of the fundraising strategy, which has made Maya pay more attention.

The relationships between our volunteers are honestly some of the best parts of this job. We have this core group of about 20 volunteers who've been with us for over two years, and they're like family. They mentor new volunteers, cover for each other during holidays, and create this amazing supportive culture. Dorothy and Frank from the Rockingham op shop have been married for 48 years and volunteer together twice a week. Seeing their partnership in action is just beautiful.

But managing volunteer dynamics can be challenging too. We've had personality conflicts, people who think their way is the only way, and occasionally someone who forgets they're working with vulnerable community members and needs coaching on appropriate behaviour. That's probably the hardest part of my job — having difficult conversations with people who are volunteering their time.

## Current Challenges

Right now I'm dealing with what feels like competing pressures from every direction. Maya and the board want us to expand our social enterprises to reduce grant dependency, but that means more volunteer coordination and probably paid staff I don't have. The Good Work Café expansion Maya's considering would require at least 15-20 additional volunteers, plus a paid coordinator I keep asking for.

I'm seeing signs of volunteer burnout that mirror what's happening with paid staff. Our core volunteers are working more hours because we're struggling to recruit enough new people. Margaret Henderson at Midland op shop is doing 12 hours a week when she used to do 6. Bob and Carol, who run our digital literacy program in Mandurah, are starting to look tired in a way that worries me.

The regional expansion pilot has created new challenges I wasn't expecting. Managing volunteers in Bunbury and Geraldton from Perth is completely different from managing metro volunteers. The technology barriers are real — some volunteers don't use email regularly, and coordinating rosters over the phone takes three times as long. I've driven to Bunbury four times this year just for volunteer meetings.

My volunteer management systems are held together with spreadsheets and prayer. I desperately need proper volunteer management software, but every quote I get comes back at $8,000-$15,000 annually. Craig keeps saying we can't justify that expense for volunteer coordination, but I'm spending 10+ hours a week on manual roster management that software could automate.

The most immediate challenge is our volunteer pipeline. We're getting fewer applications than we were two years ago — down from about 150 annually to maybe 120 this year. I think it's partly pandemic fatigue, partly increased competition from other organisations desperate for volunteers. Our information sessions are smaller, and the quality of applications feels different. People seem to want more flexible arrangements, which is harder to manage across programs that need consistent staffing.

Community events used to be my secret weapon for volunteer recruitment. Our annual Community Family Fun Day would bring 30-40 new volunteer inquiries. But event costs have gone up dramatically — insurance alone has increased by 35% since 2022. Maya's pushing me to make events more fundraising-focused, but I worry we'll lose that volunteer recruitment magic if everything becomes too commercialised.

The social enterprise expansion is keeping me awake at night. If we open two more op shops and expand the café, I'll need at least 40 additional volunteers. That's nearly doubling our volunteer workforce in 18 months. Even if I could recruit that many people, the training and coordination workload would be impossible with current staffing.

I keep pushing for a volunteer coordinator assistant or at least admin support, but the response is always about funding constraints. Meanwhile, I'm the only person in the organisation who really understands volunteer management, so if I burned out or left, the whole system would probably collapse. That's not fair to the volunteers who depend on good coordination, or to the organisation that relies on their contributions.

The hardest part is watching really good volunteers leave because they feel unsupported or undervalued. Last month we lost Sarah, who'd been coordinating our emergency relief food parcels for two years, because she felt like her suggestions for improving the system were ignored. These aren't just volunteer hours walking out the door — it's institutional knowledge and relationships that take years to build.
